title: Reading Namibia's statistics and spatial patterns

blocks.heading: Reading Namibia's statistics and spatial patterns
blocks.text:
Use a dataset's date, age group, measure and uncertainty before interpreting its map or chart. NAMPHIA surveyed households in 2017; its regional prevalence figures below concern adults aged fifteen to sixty-four, not every resident or today's population. The summary reports 7.6% in Kunene, 8.3% in Khomas, 17.9% in Ohangwena and 22.3% in Zambezi. These are estimated proportions, not counts of new infections.

![HIV prevalence among adults aged 15 to 64 in four regions, 2017, with 95 per cent intervals](../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-3.2-006-INTERP-answer.png)

blocks.text: The corresponding 95% confidence intervals are 4.9–10.3, 6.6–10.1, 16.0–19.8 and 17.5–27.0%. A chart should retain the date and age band and show uncertainty or provide it alongside the bars. The displayed point estimate in Zambezi exceeds Kunene's by 14.7 percentage points. That subtraction is not a 14.7% relative increase, and four examples do not describe every region.

In 2017 national adult prevalence was 12.6%, with Zambezi and Ohangwena above it and Kunene and Khomas below it. Zambezi borders Zambia and Botswana, and the Trans-Caprivi Highway carries freight through Katima Mulilo; Ohangwena borders Angola. These transport routes and border crossings offer a possible explanation for part of the pattern. Travel or migration can separate partners, connect sexual networks and interrupt access to prevention or treatment. These circumstances can increase exposure through unprotected sex; neither travelling nor working in a particular occupation automatically means that someone has HIV or several partners.

blocks.text: Ohangwena is densely settled, while Kunene, with lower prevalence, is very sparsely populated; but regional prevalence alone cannot establish why regions differ or which explanation matters most. It reflects past infections, age and sex composition, migration and survival on treatment. Population density and ordinary contact do not themselves transmit HIV. Unequal power in relationships can make negotiating protection harder. To test a transport-route explanation, compare evidence about exposure and access to services while accounting for these other influences; do not treat a regional correlation as proof of causation.
